objectives.title: Year 1 common exception words
objectives.rule: Some words do not sound the way they are spelled. Learn them by heart.

objectives.title: Regular plural noun suffixes -s or -es
objectives.rule: Add -s to make most words plural. Add -es to words ending in s, x, z, ch or sh.

objectives.title: Prefix un- changes the meaning of verbs and adjectives
objectives.rule: Adding un- to the start of a word gives it the opposite meaning: happy, unhappy.

objectives.title: Suffixes -ing, -ed and -er where no change is needed to the root word
objectives.rule: You can add -ing, -ed or -er to the end of many words: jump, jumping, jumped, jumper.

objectives.title: Joining words and clauses using and
objectives.rule: Use and to join two words or two ideas together.

objectives.title: Capital letters and full stops to demarcate sentences
objectives.rule: A sentence starts with a capital letter and usually ends with a full stop.

objectives.title: Question marks and exclamation marks
objectives.rule: A question ends with a question mark. An exclamation mark shows strong feeling.

objectives.title: Capital letters for names and the personal pronoun I
objectives.rule: Names of people, places and days start with a capital letter. The word I is always a capital.

objectives.title: Year 2 common exception words
objectives.rule: Some words do not follow the usual sound rules. Learn them by heart.

objectives.title: Forming nouns with -ness and -er, adjectives with -ful and -less, and adverbs with -ly
objectives.rule: Suffixes change a word's job: kind (adjective) becomes kindness (noun) and kindly (adverb).

objectives.title: Coordination (or, and, but) and subordination (when, if, that, because)
objectives.rule: Conjunctions join ideas. And, but and or join equal ideas. When, if, that and because add extra information.

objectives.title: Statements, questions, exclamations and commands
objectives.rule: A statement tells, a question asks, a command orders and an exclamation starts with what or how.

objectives.title: Present and past tense, including the progressive form
objectives.rule: Verbs change to show when something happens: I play (present), I played (past), I am playing (progressive).

objectives.title: Expanded noun phrases for description and specification
objectives.rule: Add adjectives before a noun to describe it: the big, blue butterfly.

objectives.title: Commas to separate items in a list
objectives.rule: Put commas between items in a list. Use and (not a comma) before the last item.

objectives.title: Apostrophes to mark where letters are missing
objectives.rule: An apostrophe shows where letters have been left out: do not becomes don't.

objectives.title: Apostrophes for singular possession in nouns
objectives.rule: Add 's to show something belongs to one person or thing: the girl's coat.

objectives.title: Year 3 and 4 statutory spelling list
objectives.rule: These are words you need to know how to spell by the end of Year 4.

objectives.title: Prefixes such as super-, anti-, auto-, dis-, mis-, re-, sub- and inter-
objectives.rule: A prefix goes at the start of a word and changes its meaning: re- means again, dis- and mis- often mean not or wrongly.

objectives.title: Word families based on common words
objectives.rule: Words in a family share a root word and are linked in meaning: solve, solution, solver.

objectives.title: Using a or an according to whether the next word begins with a consonant or a vowel
objectives.rule: Use an before a vowel sound (an apple, an hour) and a before a consonant sound (a banana).

objectives.title: Expressing time, place and cause using conjunctions, adverbs and prepositions
objectives.rule: Words like before, after, because, soon, under and during tell us when, where or why something happens.

objectives.title: The present perfect form of verbs
objectives.rule: The present perfect uses has or have with a verb: She has finished. They have gone.

objectives.title: Introduction to inverted commas to punctuate direct speech
objectives.rule: Inverted commas go around the words someone actually says.

objectives.title: Fronted adverbials
objectives.rule: A fronted adverbial is a word or phrase at the start of a sentence that tells you when, where or how something happened.

objectives.title: Use of commas after fronted adverbials
objectives.rule: Put a comma after a fronted adverbial: After lunch, we went outside.

objectives.title: Use of inverted commas and other punctuation to indicate direct speech
objectives.rule: Put inverted commas around spoken words. The punctuation that ends the speech goes inside the inverted commas.

objectives.title: Apostrophes to mark plural possession
objectives.rule: If a plural ends in s, add just an apostrophe: the girls' coats. If it does not, add 's: the children's coats.

objectives.title: Standard English forms for verb inflections
objectives.rule: In Standard English we say we were (not we was) and I did (not I done).

objectives.title: Noun phrases expanded by modifying adjectives, nouns and prepositional phrases
objectives.rule: A noun phrase can grow with adjectives and a prepositional phrase: the old teacher with curly hair.

objectives.title: Appropriate choice of pronoun or noun to aid cohesion and avoid repetition
objectives.rule: A pronoun (he, she, it, they, them) can replace a noun so you do not repeat it, as long as it stays clear who you mean.

objectives.title: Determiners
objectives.rule: A determiner comes before a noun and tells you which one or how many: the, a, this, those, some, my, three.

objectives.title: Homophones and near-homophones
objectives.rule: Homophones sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things: whether and weather.

objectives.title: Suffixes -ation, -ous, -ly, -tion, -sion, -ssion and -cian
objectives.rule: Many word endings sound alike. -cian is used for people's jobs (musician); -sion often follows d or s (explosion).

objectives.title: Year 5 and 6 statutory spelling list
objectives.rule: These are words you need to know how to spell by the end of Year 6.

objectives.title: Relative clauses beginning with who, which, where, when, whose or that
objectives.rule: A relative clause adds information about a noun and starts with who, which, where, when, whose or that.

objectives.title: Modal verbs to indicate degrees of possibility
objectives.rule: Modal verbs such as might, could, should, will and must show how likely or necessary something is.

objectives.title: Adverbs to indicate degrees of possibility
objectives.rule: Adverbs such as perhaps, surely, definitely and possibly show how certain we are.

objectives.title: Brackets, dashes or commas to indicate parenthesis
objectives.rule: Put extra information in a pair of brackets, dashes or commas. The sentence still makes sense without it.

objectives.title: Commas to clarify meaning or avoid ambiguity
objectives.rule: A comma can change what a sentence means: Let's eat, Grandma! is not the same as Let's eat Grandma!

objectives.title: Converting nouns or adjectives into verbs using -ate, -ise, -ify and -en
objectives.rule: Suffixes can turn a word into a verb: active becomes activate, apology becomes apologise, solid becomes solidify, wide becomes widen.

objectives.title: Verb prefixes dis-, de-, mis-, over- and re-
objectives.rule: Prefixes change a verb's meaning: re- means again, mis- means wrongly, over- means too much.

objectives.title: Use of the passive to affect the presentation of information
objectives.rule: In the passive, the thing the action happens to comes first: The window was broken (by the ball).

objectives.title: The subjunctive form in formal writing
objectives.rule: The subjunctive is used in very formal writing: If I were you... I insist that he be on time.

objectives.title: Formal and informal vocabulary and structures
objectives.rule: Formal writing avoids slang and contractions: request instead of ask for, do not instead of don't.

objectives.title: How words are related by meaning as synonyms and antonyms
objectives.rule: Synonyms have similar meanings (big, large). Antonyms have opposite meanings (big, small).

objectives.title: Semi-colons to mark the boundary between independent clauses
objectives.rule: A semi-colon joins two closely linked main clauses that could each be a sentence.

objectives.title: Colons to introduce a list or mark the boundary between independent clauses
objectives.rule: A colon introduces a list or an explanation. What comes before it must be a full sentence.

objectives.title: Hyphens to avoid ambiguity
objectives.rule: A hyphen joins words to make meaning clear: man-eating shark, re-cover the sofa.

objectives.title: Word classes: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions and determiners
objectives.rule: The same word can be a different word class depending on the job it does in the sentence.

objectives.title: Main clauses and subordinate clauses
objectives.rule: A main clause makes sense on its own. A subordinate clause adds information but does not make sense on its own.
